{{Short description|Elliptic curve}}
[[Image:Mordell curve example.png|thumb|right|<math>y^2 = x^3 + 1</math>, with solutions at <math>(-1, 0)</math>, <math>(0, 1)</math> and <math>(0, -1)</math>]]

In [[algebra]], a '''Mordell curve''' is an [[elliptic curve]] of the form <math>y^2 = x^3 + n</math>, where <math>n</math> is a fixed non-zero [[integer]].<ref name="wolfram">{{MathWorld |urlname=MordellCurve |title=Mordell Curve}}</ref>

These curves were closely studied by [[Louis Mordell]],<ref>{{cite book |author=Louis Mordell |title=Diophantine Equations |year=1969|author-link=Louis Mordell }}</ref> from the point of view of determining their integer points. He showed that every Mordell curve contains only finitely many integer points <math>(x, y)</math>. In other words, the differences of [[square number|perfect squares]] and [[perfect cube]]s tend to infinity. The question of how fast was dealt with in principle by [[Baker's method]]. Hypothetically this issue is dealt with by [[Marshall Hall's conjecture]].

==Properties==
*If <math>(x, y)</math> is an integer point on a Mordell curve, then so is <math>(x, -y)</math>.
*If <math>(x, y)</math> is a rational point on a Mordell curve with <math>y \ne 0</math>, then so is <math>\left( \frac{x^4 - 8nx}{4y^2}, \frac{-x^6 - 20nx^3 + 8n^2}{8y^3} \right)</math>. Moreover, if <math>xy \ne 0</math> and <math>n</math> is not 1 or −432, an infinite number of rational solutions can be generated this way. This formula is known as '''Bachet's duplication formula'''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Silverman |first1=Joseph |author-link1=Joseph H. Silverman |last2=Tate |first2=John |author-link2=John Tate (mathematician) |date=1992 |title=Rational Points on Elliptic Curves |edition=2nd|chapter = Introduction| pages=xvi}}</ref>
*When <math>n \ne 0</math>, the Mordell curve only has finitely many integer solutions (see [[Siegel's theorem on integral points]]).
*There are certain values of <math>n</math> for which the corresponding Mordell curve has no integer solutions;<ref name="wolfram" /> these values are:
: 6, 7, 11, 13, 14, 20, 21, 23, 29, 32, 34, 39, 42, ... {{OEIS|A054504}}.
: −3, −5, −6, −9, −10, −12, −14, −16, −17, −21, −22, ... {{OEIS|A081121}}.

*The specific case where <math>n = -2</math> is also known as '''Fermat's Sandwich Theorem'''.<ref>{{MathWorld |title=Fermat's Sandwich Theorem |id=FermatsSandwichTheorem |access-date=24 March 2022}}</ref>

In 1998, J. Gebel, A. Pethö, H. G. Zimmer found all integers points for <math>0<|n| \le 10^4</math>.<ref>{{cite journal | title = On Mordell's equation | doi=10.1023/A:1000281602647 | volume=110 | issue=3 | journal=Compositio Mathematica | pages=335–367|year = 1998|last1 = Gebel|first1 = J.| last2=Pethö | first2=A. | last3=Zimmer | first3=H. G. | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>Sequences {{OEIS2C|1=A081119}} and {{OEIS2C|A081120}}.</ref>

In 2015, M. A. Bennett and A. Ghadermarzi computed integer points for <math>0<|n| \le 10^7</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |author=M. A. Bennett, A. Ghadermarzi |title=Mordell's equation : a classical approach |journal=LMS Journal of Computation and Mathematics |volume=18 |year=2015 |pages=633–646 |doi=10.1112/S1461157015000182 |arxiv=1311.7077 |url=http://www.math.ubc.ca/~bennett/BeGh-LMSJCM-2015.pdf}}</ref>
